analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program run through Social Security.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill with 38 cosponsors — 37 of 45 Democrats and 1 of 2 independents, no Republicans — would create a federal paid family and medical leave benefit of up to $4,000 a month; it has sat in the Finance Committee with no action since its September 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would create a national paid family and medical leave insurance program run by the Social Security Administration. Workers who need time off for their own serious health condition, to care for a wide circle of family members, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking would receive monthly cash benefits replacing most of their wages, up to $4,000 a month. It would also protect their jobs while they are out and pay federal grants to states that already run their own paid leave programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need leave — for a new child, their own serious illness, or a family member's care — would gain a cash benefit that does not exist at the federal level today. The bill covers part-time and self-employed people: you qualify with just $2,000 of earnings over the prior eight quarters [S2]. Benefits replace 85% of the first roughly $1,257 of monthly earnings, phasing down to 50% of earnings above about $6,200, with a floor of $580 and a cap of $4,000 per month, indexed to wage growth [S2]. Each person can use up to 12 times their regular weekly hours per 12-month period — effectively 12 weeks for a full-time worker [S2]. Employers must reinstate workers to the same or an equivalent job, keep their health coverage going, and face a presumption of retaliation for any adverse action within 12 months of leave [S2]. States that already run paid leave programs keep operating and get federal grants covering their costs [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers needing family or medical leave

how_it_helps.text: Creates a national paid leave insurance benefit — up to 12 times a worker's regular weekly hours per year, effectively 12 paid weeks for a full-time worker — covering the worker's own serious health condition, care for a broad set of family members including domestic partners, siblings, and chosen family, and needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or sex trafficking [S2].

Replaces most lost wages: 85% of earnings up to about $1,257 a month, 69% of the next tier, and 50% above roughly $6,200, paying between $580 and $4,000 per month, with amounts indexed to wage growth [S2].
Covers part-time, seasonal, and self-employed workers — the earnings test is only $2,000 over the prior eight quarters — and applications can be filed starting 18 months after enactment [S2].

Protects the job: employers must restore the worker to the same or an equivalent position, maintain health coverage during leave, and any adverse action within 12 months of leave is presumed retaliatory unless the employer proves otherwise [S2].
Preserves existing state paid leave programs and funds them: 'legacy states' keep their own programs and receive federal grants covering the full cost of their state benefits and administration [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The bill is built as social insurance financed through the payroll tax system — its wage definitions are keyed to the same tax-code sections that govern Social Security payroll taxes [S2] — and benefits are paid from a newly created federal Family and Medical Leave Insurance Trust Fund [S2]. The portion of the bill text provided does not spell out the contribution rate, so the exact split between workers and employers is not visible in the record. The Social Security Administration would bear the cost of running a new Office of Paid Family and Medical Leave [S2]. Employers take on compliance duties: notices, recordkeeping, and exposure to lawsuits with double damages and attorney's fees if they retaliate [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers through payroll financing

drawbacks.text: The financing is not visible in the bill text provided: the bill creates a new federal trust fund and keys its wage definitions to the Social Security payroll tax sections, but the excerpt does not show a contribution rate, so the annual cost to workers and employers cannot be read from the record [S2].

The 12-month rebuttable presumption of retaliation is broad: any firing, demotion, or discipline in the year after leave can be treated as retaliation unless the employer proves otherwise, which raises legal risk and compliance costs, especially for small businesses [S2].

Program integrity leans on self-reported monthly 'caregiving hours': applications and monthly reports are presumed true unless the Commissioner proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence, and the family definition reaches chosen family related 'by affinity', so fraud prevention depends heavily on enforcement by a new federal office [S2].

Higher earners get thinner coverage — 50% replacement on earnings above roughly $6,200 a month — so a mid-career professional taking 12 weeks could see a substantial income drop despite the $4,000 monthly cap [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is large and concrete: the United States has no federal paid family or medical leave, and this bill would create one that covers part-time and self-employed workers, pays most of a low-wage worker's salary, and comes with real job protection. The honest costs are real but less visible in this record: the contribution rate that finances the trust fund is not shown in the provided text, the retaliation presumption creates genuine litigation exposure for employers, and anti-fraud enforcement depends on a new office that must be stood up from scratch. On balance, the bill's design follows the model of state programs that have operated for years, but its price tag cannot be confirmed from the materials provided.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote; the congressional session runs through early January 2027, so it is still technically alive.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the FAMILY Act on September 16, 2025, with 38 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day [S1] [S4].
All 38 cosponsors are Democrats or independents — 37 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents; not a single Senate Republican signed on [S3].
Since the referral, the action record shows nothing further: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote [S4].
With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and the chairmanship of the Finance Committee, the bill's path to the floor runs entirely through the majority, which has taken no action on it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody yet — the bill has not been voted up or down, so no group has gained or lost from any action taken on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill waits in committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, but the sponsorship is entirely partisan: 37 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents signed on, and none of the 55 Senate Republicans did.

industries.note: A universal public benefit displaces the private paid-leave and disability insurance products these companies sell to employers. In states that already run their own programs, employer-purchased coverage keeps counting and can receive a share of federal grants, softening the loss there [S2].

Employers would pay into the new trust fund through the payroll system and take on notice, reinstatement, health-coverage, and anti-retaliation duties with lawsuit exposure — costs that are the flip side of the benefit workers gain [S2].

industries.industry: State paid-leave programs (e.g., California, New York, New Jersey, Washington)
industries.note: States with existing programs keep running them and are paid federal grants covering the full cost of benefits and administration, locking in their role as administrators rather than folding them into the federal system [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds. With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats, the Finance chairmanship, and control of the floor calendar, and with zero Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or markup this session. Versions of this bill have been introduced in past Congresses without reaching a floor vote, and the most common fate for a Senate bill of this kind is to remain in committee until the session ends in January 2027.
